overview.what_it_is: Re-order Paragraphs is a PTE Academic reading task in which several text boxes from one academic passage are presented in the wrong order. The learner must reconstruct the single logical sequence by identifying the opening sentence, connecting dependent sentences, building strong adjacent pairs, and checking the paragraph's overall development.

format_facts.label: Passage length
format_facts.value: The source lesson describes passages of up to approximately 150 words.

format_facts.label: Number of items
format_facts.value: The source lesson indicates that test takers may encounter two to three Re-order Paragraphs items.

format_facts.label: Response method
format_facts.value: Move the text boxes until they form one coherent academic paragraph.

format_facts.label: Correct sequence
format_facts.value: Each item has one intended order based on meaning, grammar, reference, and discourse structure.

format_facts.label: Timing
format_facts.value: The reading section is timed as a whole, so this item is not normally timed separately.

format_facts.label: Text style
format_facts.value: Passages commonly follow academic patterns such as general-to-specific explanation, chronological development, cause and effect, comparison, classification, or problem and solution.

scoring_factors.name: Correct adjacent pairs
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether one text box is placed immediately before the text box that logically follows it.

scoring_factors.name: Sequence reconstruction
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: The ability to rebuild the passage's intended progression from introduction through development to conclusion.

scoring_factors.name: Reading comprehension
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Understanding of the topic, main idea, supporting details, relationships, and implied connections.

scoring_factors.name: Cohesion recognition
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Recognition of links created by articles, pronouns, repeated vocabulary, synonyms, discourse markers, and grammatical dependencies.

critical_rules: Find a sentence that can introduce the topic independently; do not automatically choose the shortest or most general-looking sentence.
A sentence containing an unexplained pronoun, definite reference, contrast marker, example marker, or conclusion marker is usually dependent on earlier information.
Build reliable two-sentence links before attempting to solve the entire sequence.
Use several kinds of evidence together; meaning alone can create more than one plausible order.
Check that every pronoun and reference phrase has a clear antecedent.
Check that new information is introduced before it is treated as known information.
Prefer the order that produces both local cohesion between neighbours and global coherence across the complete paragraph.
Do not spend excessive time forcing one uncertain link; preserve strong pairs and return to the weaker connection.

learning_goals: Identify a topic sentence that introduces the passage without depending on earlier context.
Distinguish topic sentences from supporting sentences, examples, explanations, and conclusions.
Use indefinite and definite articles to track first mention and later reference.
Use pronouns, demonstratives, and other referents to connect sentences accurately.
Recognize discourse markers that signal addition, contrast, similarity, example, cause, result, sequence, and conclusion.
Identify repeated nouns, synonyms, related vocabulary, and lexical chains across sentences.
Recognize common academic paragraph structures such as general-to-specific, chronological, cause-and-effect, and problem-solution development.
Build strong adjacent pairs before deciding the full order.
Reject possible orders that contain unresolved references or logical jumps.
Complete Re-order Paragraphs items efficiently under reading-section time pressure.
Explain why each sentence follows the previous one instead of relying on intuition alone.
Review mistakes by identifying the clue that was missed, misread, or overvalued.

core_method.name: The OPEN-LINK-CHECK Method
core_method.summary: First locate the most independent opening sentence. Next, identify sentences that clearly depend on earlier information. Build strong adjacent links using grammar, reference, vocabulary, and logic. Finally, assemble the complete paragraph and check that it develops naturally from introduction to conclusion.

steps.detail: Read all text boxes quickly for the shared topic, text type, and likely organizational pattern. Do not begin moving boxes after reading only one sentence.
Choose the sentence that names or introduces the central subject and does not contain an unexplained backward reference such as this, these, they, the process, however, or therefore.
Identify sentences that require earlier information because they contain pronouns, definite noun phrases, examples, contrasts, results, comparisons, or conclusions.
Create high-confidence links such as a named noun followed by its pronoun, a general claim followed by an example, a cause followed by its result, or a first mention followed by a definite reference.
Combine compatible pairs into longer sequences while protecting links supported by multiple clues.
For remaining sentences, compare which position best satisfies reference, chronology, tense, vocabulary continuity, and paragraph structure.
Read the complete sequence as one paragraph and confirm that the topic is introduced, developed, illustrated or explained, and appropriately completed.
Check every article, pronoun, discourse marker, repeated concept, and time expression before submitting.

core_method.formula: Independent opener + strong adjacent pairs + complete reference chains + logical paragraph development = most reliable order

techniques.name: Topic-Sentence Test
techniques.purpose: To identify the most likely opening sentence.
how_to: Look for the sentence that introduces the central subject by name.
Prefer a sentence that can be understood without information from another box.
Check whether it presents a broad claim, definition, situation, or historical starting point.
Reject sentences beginning with unexplained backward references or transition markers.
Confirm that the remaining sentences can naturally develop its main idea.
techniques.example: Urban farming has become increasingly common in densely populated cities. This can open a paragraph because it introduces the subject directly. By contrast, 'This practice offers several benefits' cannot open because 'This practice' has not yet been identified.
techniques.why_it_matters: A correct opener establishes the topic and narrows the number of possible sequences.
techniques.common_error: Choosing a sentence as the opener merely because it sounds important, even though it contains a hidden reference to earlier information.

techniques.name: New-to-Known Article Tracking
techniques.purpose: To follow how a noun is first introduced and later referred to as known information.
how_to: Look for first mentions using a, an, a named entity, or a full noun phrase.
Look for later mentions using the, this, that, these, those, or a shortened noun phrase.
Place the introduction before the later reference.
Check whether the definite noun has a unique or previously identified meaning.
Do not apply the rule mechanically when the noun is already unique, such as the sun.
techniques.example: A research team developed a new water filter. The filter removed most contaminants. The first sentence introduces the filter; the second treats it as known information.
techniques.why_it_matters: Articles provide grammatical evidence about information order and often create a strong adjacent pair.
techniques.common_error: Assuming that every sentence containing 'the' must come later, without checking whether the noun is naturally unique or already defined by context.

techniques.name: Pronoun and Referent Mapping
techniques.purpose: To connect dependent sentences to the nouns or ideas they refer to.
how_to: Circle pronouns and reference phrases such as it, they, them, this, these, such a method, and the former.
Search earlier boxes for a noun matching the pronoun's number and meaning.
Confirm that the antecedent is specific enough to make the reference clear.
Place the referent sentence after the sentence that introduces its antecedent.
Check whether the reference points to one noun, a whole event, or an entire previous idea.
techniques.example: Researchers tested two teaching methods. They found that collaborative learning produced better retention. 'They' refers to the plural noun 'researchers'.
techniques.why_it_matters: A pronoun without a clear antecedent is one of the strongest signs that a sentence cannot stand first.
techniques.common_error: Linking a pronoun to the nearest noun even when the number, meaning, or logical role does not match.

techniques.name: Discourse-Marker Decoding
techniques.purpose: To recognize the logical relationship between neighbouring sentences.
how_to: Classify the marker by function rather than reading it as an isolated word.
For however or nevertheless, find a previous idea that can be contrasted.
For therefore, thus, or as a result, find the cause or evidence that produces the result.
For for example or for instance, find the general claim being illustrated.
For in conclusion or overall, place the sentence after the main discussion.
techniques.example: Online courses offer greater flexibility. However, some learners miss face-to-face interaction. The contrast marker requires the positive claim to appear before the limitation.
techniques.why_it_matters: Discourse markers reveal the writer's intended relationship between ideas and often identify sentence direction.
techniques.common_error: Treating a marker as a decorative connector rather than asking what earlier idea it depends on.

techniques.name: Lexical-Chain Tracking
techniques.purpose: To follow one concept as it is repeated, renamed, classified, or paraphrased.
how_to: Underline repeated content words across the boxes.
Group synonyms and related expressions, such as pollution, emissions, and air quality.
Notice movement from a full technical term to a shorter expression.
Use vocabulary continuity to support a possible pair.
Combine lexical evidence with grammar and logic before finalizing the link.
techniques.example: The paragraph may move from 'renewable energy technologies' to 'these systems' and later to 'solar and wind power'. These expressions form one lexical chain.
techniques.why_it_matters: Academic texts often avoid exact repetition, so recognizing paraphrase is essential for following topic development.
techniques.common_error: Rejecting a correct link because the two sentences do not repeat exactly the same noun.

techniques.name: General-to-Specific Structure
techniques.purpose: To recognize a common academic progression from a broad statement to details, evidence, or examples.
how_to: Locate the broad claim, definition, or overview.
Identify sentences that explain parts of that claim.
Place examples after the idea they illustrate.
Place statistics or research findings after the topic they support.
Check whether the paragraph becomes progressively more specific.
techniques.example: Many factors influence sleep quality. One important factor is exposure to artificial light. For example, phone screens can delay the release of melatonin.
techniques.why_it_matters: Many PTE passages follow a predictable academic pattern that can resolve otherwise ambiguous links.
techniques.common_error: Placing an interesting example before the general idea that gives the example meaning.

techniques.name: Chronology and Process Sequencing
techniques.purpose: To order events, stages, discoveries, or procedures according to time.
how_to: Mark dates, time expressions, verb tenses, and stage markers.
Identify the earliest event or initial stage.
Follow expressions such as initially, later, subsequently, and eventually.
Check whether one event creates the conditions for the next.
Distinguish chronological order from the order in which the sentences are visually presented.
techniques.example: First, the samples are collected. They are then stored at a low temperature. Finally, the material is analyzed in a laboratory.
techniques.why_it_matters: Time and process markers can produce a nearly fixed sequence.
techniques.common_error: Following repeated vocabulary while ignoring a clear contradiction in dates or procedural stages.

techniques.name: Cause-and-Effect Linking
techniques.purpose: To connect reasons, conditions, consequences, and conclusions.
how_to: Identify cause language such as because, since, owing to, and due to.
Identify result language such as therefore, consequently, thus, and as a result.
Place the cause before a backward-pointing result sentence.
Check whether the result logically follows from the stated evidence.
Distinguish a cause from an example or simple sequence.
techniques.example: The region experienced several years of low rainfall. Consequently, water reserves fell to historically low levels.
techniques.why_it_matters: Cause-and-effect chains commonly organize short academic paragraphs.
techniques.common_error: Placing a consequence before the reason simply because both sentences discuss the same topic.

techniques.name: Pair-First Assembly
techniques.purpose: To reduce cognitive load by solving dependable local links before the whole paragraph.
how_to: Search for the strongest two-sentence relationship.
Prefer pairs supported by at least two clues.
Record each pair as a fixed block.
Join blocks only when the boundary between them is also coherent.
Reopen a pair only when the complete paragraph produces a contradiction.
techniques.example: A sentence introducing 'a hotel' followed by one beginning 'That hotel' forms a stronger pair than two sentences connected only by a broad shared topic.
techniques.why_it_matters: PTE scoring rewards correct neighbouring relationships, and pair building prevents random full-sequence guessing.
techniques.common_error: Trying to solve all five boxes simultaneously and repeatedly changing correct links.

techniques.name: Global Coherence Check
techniques.purpose: To confirm that locally correct pairs also form one complete and purposeful paragraph.
how_to: Read the proposed order without looking at the original labels.
Summarize the function of each sentence in one or two words.
Check for a sensible pattern such as topic, explanation, example, result, conclusion.
Look for abrupt topic changes or repeated introductions.
Confirm that the final sentence feels like a natural endpoint rather than a new beginning.
techniques.example: An order may contain two grammatical pairs but still fail globally if a conclusion appears before the evidence it summarizes.
techniques.why_it_matters: Local clues can occasionally support more than one arrangement; global structure resolves the final ambiguity.
techniques.common_error: Submitting as soon as all pronouns are resolved without checking the overall argument.

worked_examples.title: Worked Example 1: Articles and References in a Building Description
worked_examples.input: A. A hotel occupying several upper floors will provide accommodation for visitors. B. The Burj Dubai was designed to become one of the world's tallest buildings. C. That hotel will also include restaurants and leisure facilities. D. The building's final height was initially estimated rather than publicly confirmed. E. The use of the word 'estimated' reflected uncertainty about the final measurement.
worked_examples.decoding: Sentence B introduces the named building and can stand independently, so it is the opener. Sentence D uses 'The building', which refers back to the Burj Dubai. Sentence E explains the expression 'estimated' from D. Sentence A introduces new information with 'A hotel'. Sentence C begins with 'That hotel', so it must follow A.
worked_examples.plan: First secure B-D through the named-building to definite-reference link. Next secure D-E through the repeated word 'estimated'. Finally secure A-C through first mention and demonstrative reference. Join the chains as B-D-E-A-C because the text moves from the building generally to one feature inside it.
worked_examples.model_answer: Correct order: B → D → E → A → C

annotations.comment: The proper name introduces the subject; 'The building' refers back to it.
The phrase 'the word estimated' directly explains wording used in D.
After the discussion of height is complete, the paragraph introduces a new feature with the indefinite article 'A'.
'That hotel' cannot appear until the hotel has been introduced.

worked_examples.title: Worked Example 2: Referents in a Historical Paragraph
worked_examples.input: A. This pagan festival was held in the middle of February and celebrated fertility. B. Valentine's Day is now associated with cards, flowers, and romantic messages. C. This early Pope attempted to replace the older celebration with a Christian observance. D. The holiday may have developed partly from an ancient Roman festival. E. Pope Gelasius I later opposed the continuing pagan tradition.
worked_examples.decoding: Sentence B names Valentine's Day and introduces the modern topic. Sentence D uses 'The holiday', referring back to Valentine's Day. Sentence A uses 'This pagan festival', referring to the ancient Roman festival in D. Sentence E introduces Pope Gelasius I. Sentence C then uses 'This early Pope' to refer back to him.
worked_examples.plan: Build the reference chain B-D-A, then the proper-name chain E-C. Join them chronologically: the festival is introduced before the Pope's response to it.
worked_examples.model_answer: Correct order: B → D → A → E → C

annotations.comment: 'The holiday' has a clear antecedent only after Valentine's Day is named.
'This pagan festival' points to the ancient Roman festival.
The pagan tradition must be described before the paragraph discusses opposition to it.
'This early Pope' refers specifically to Pope Gelasius I.

worked_examples.title: Worked Example 3: General Claim, Evidence, and Result
worked_examples.input: A. As a result, some universities have begun creating compulsory digital-literacy courses. B. Many first-year students are confident users of social media. C. For example, some struggle to judge whether an online source is academically reliable. D. However, frequent use of digital platforms does not always produce strong academic research skills. E. These courses teach students how to evaluate sources, protect data, and cite digital material.
worked_examples.decoding: Sentence B introduces students' digital experience. Sentence D begins with 'However' and contrasts social-media confidence with limited research ability. Sentence C gives an example of the weakness described in D. Sentence A presents an institutional result of that problem. Sentence E uses 'These courses' to explain the courses introduced in A.
worked_examples.plan: Identify the contrast pair B-D, the claim-example pair D-C, and the new-reference pair A-E. Connect C to A because the student difficulty motivates the institutional response.
worked_examples.model_answer: Correct order: B → D → C → A → E

annotations.comment: The contrast marker 'However' requires an earlier positive-looking statement.
'For example' introduces a specific illustration of weak research skills.
The difficulty provides the cause for the universities' response.
'These courses' refers to the compulsory digital-literacy courses.

worked_examples.title: Worked Example 4: Chronological Scientific Process
worked_examples.input: A. The resulting measurements are then compared with records from previous years. B. Scientists first place monitoring instruments at selected points across the glacier. C. Finally, the comparison allows researchers to estimate how rapidly the glacier is changing. D. During the summer, the instruments record changes in height and movement. E. This equipment must remain stable despite severe weather conditions.
worked_examples.decoding: Sentence B introduces the instruments and marks the first stage. Sentence E uses 'This equipment', referring to those instruments. Sentence D explains what the instruments do during the monitoring period. Sentence A begins with 'The resulting measurements', which come from D. Sentence C begins with 'Finally' and states the final analytical outcome.
worked_examples.plan: Follow the process from installation to equipment requirements, data collection, comparison, and conclusion.
worked_examples.model_answer: Correct order: B → E → D → A → C

annotations.comment: 'This equipment' refers to the monitoring instruments introduced in B.
After the equipment is established, the paragraph explains the data it records.
'The resulting measurements' are the measurements produced during recording.
'Finally' signals the last stage and explains the purpose of the comparison.

worked_examples.title: Worked Example 5: Eliminating a False Opener
worked_examples.input: A. These findings challenged the common belief that longer meetings produce better decisions. B. A recent workplace study examined how meeting length affects group performance. C. In the experiment, teams were given either thirty or ninety minutes to solve the same problem. D. The shorter meetings produced decisions of equal quality in considerably less time. E. Therefore, the researchers recommended setting strict limits on routine meetings.
worked_examples.decoding: Sentence A sounds important but cannot open because 'These findings' has no antecedent. Sentence B independently introduces the study. Sentence C explains its design. Sentence D reports the findings. Sentence A interprets those findings, and E gives the resulting recommendation.
worked_examples.plan: Use the standard research structure: study introduction, method, result, interpretation, recommendation.
worked_examples.model_answer: Correct order: B → C → D → A → E

annotations.comment: This is the independent topic sentence and names the research focus.
The phrase 'In the experiment' develops the study introduced in B.
The result can only be understood after the two meeting conditions are described.
'These findings' refers to the result reported in D.
'Therefore' introduces the recommendation arising from the evidence.

items.item: This order creates a logical jump because...
items.when_to_use: Reject a transition that changes topic, time, or argument without support.

items.item: Both orders are grammatical, but this one is more coherent because...
items.when_to_use: Resolve ambiguity through paragraph structure and information development.

common_mistakes.mistake: Choosing a sentence with a definite article as the opener without checking its noun.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The noun may refer to something that must be introduced in an earlier sentence.
common_mistakes.fix: Ask whether the noun is uniquely identifiable or whether it depends on a previous first mention.

common_mistakes.mistake: Ignoring pronouns because the general topic seems obvious.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: A pronoun requires a precise antecedent, not merely a sentence about the same broad subject.
common_mistakes.fix: Match every pronoun with a specific noun or idea and check number, meaning, and grammatical role.

common_mistakes.mistake: Ordering sentences only through repeated keywords.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The same word may appear in several sentences without indicating direct adjacency.
common_mistakes.fix: Use vocabulary repetition as supporting evidence alongside reference, grammar, and logic.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating discourse markers as optional decoration.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Words such as however, therefore, and for example impose a specific relationship with previous information.
common_mistakes.fix: Name the marker's function and identify the exact sentence that supplies the required contrast, cause, or claim.

common_mistakes.mistake: Placing an example before the general statement it illustrates.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The reader encounters detail without knowing its purpose or category.
common_mistakes.fix: Place for example, for instance, and specific cases after the broader claim.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming that the topic sentence must always be the broadest sentence.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: A broad sentence may still contain an unresolved reference or function as a conclusion.
common_mistakes.fix: Test both independence and introductory function, not breadth alone.

common_mistakes.mistake: Solving the whole order by intuition in one attempt.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: This overloads working memory and makes correct links easy to lose.
common_mistakes.fix: Build and protect high-confidence adjacent pairs before assembling the full chain.

common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Two sentences may be grammatically compatible but historically or procedurally reversed.
common_mistakes.fix: Mark dates, stages, tense changes, and time expressions before finalizing the sequence.

common_mistakes.mistake: Refusing to reconsider an early pair.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: A locally plausible pair may create an impossible global paragraph.
common_mistakes.fix: Keep strong pairs provisionally, but reopen them when the full sequence creates a reference or logic contradiction.

common_mistakes.mistake: Spending too long on one uncertain boundary.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Reading-section time is shared across several item types.
common_mistakes.fix: Secure the strongest pairs, select the most coherent remaining order, and move on after a final check.

time_budget.focus: Review the format, purpose, adjacent-pair scoring concept, and common paragraph structures.
Separate independent openers from dependent sentences containing backward references.
Track first mention, later reference, pronouns, demonstratives, and renamed concepts.
Classify linkers by function and connect each marker to the information it requires.
Build high-confidence adjacent pairs using two or more clues.
Solve complete items and explain the role of every sentence.
Complete several items efficiently without sacrificing reference and coherence checks.
Record the missed clue and the strategy needed to prevent the same mistake.

drills.name: Opener or Dependent?
drills.instructions: Collect ten sentences from academic paragraphs. Label each as a possible opener or a dependent sentence. Underline the exact word that creates dependency.

drills.name: Article Chain
drills.instructions: Create pairs using patterns such as 'a device' followed by 'the device', or a proper name followed by a shortened definite reference.

drills.name: Pronoun Hunt
drills.instructions: For each pronoun or demonstrative, identify its antecedent and explain why competing nouns cannot be the referent.

drills.name: Marker Match
drills.instructions: Match sentences beginning with however, therefore, for example, similarly, and finally to suitable preceding sentences.

drills.name: Lexical Chain
drills.instructions: Underline exact repetition, synonyms, category-member relationships, and full-term-to-short-form references across a paragraph.

drills.name: Strongest Pair First
drills.instructions: Given five boxes, identify only the strongest adjacent pair. Require at least two reasons before accepting the pair.

drills.name: Paragraph Function Labels
drills.instructions: After ordering an item, label each sentence as topic, explanation, example, evidence, contrast, result, or conclusion.

drills.name: Broken Order Diagnosis
drills.instructions: Study an incorrect sequence and identify the first point where reference, chronology, or logic breaks.

drills.name: Two-Possibility Comparison
drills.instructions: When two orders seem possible, write one sentence explaining why one has stronger local cohesion and global coherence.

drills.name: Timed Three-Item Set
drills.instructions: Complete three items in a fixed practice window, mark uncertain links, and review accuracy by adjacent pair rather than only by complete order.

practice_plan.routine: For every item, spend a few seconds previewing all boxes, identify the independent opener, mark dependent language, build two or three strong pairs, assemble the chain, and perform one final read for reference, chronology, and paragraph purpose. During review, record whether the error came from the opener, an article, a referent, a discourse marker, vocabulary continuity, chronology, or global structure.

mastery_checklist: I can explain what Re-order Paragraphs tests and how the response is constructed.
I can identify a likely opener without relying only on sentence length or position.
I can distinguish a topic sentence from an example, contrast, result, or conclusion.
I can track first mention with a, an, or a full noun phrase and later reference with the or a demonstrative.
I can identify the antecedent of it, they, this, these, that, those, and similar reference phrases.
I can explain the function of addition, contrast, example, cause, result, sequence, and conclusion markers.
I can recognize lexical chains formed through repetition, synonyms, and related academic vocabulary.
I can recognize general-to-specific, chronological, cause-effect, comparison, and problem-solution structures.
I can build reliable adjacent pairs using at least two clues.
I can reject an order that contains an unresolved pronoun or definite reference.
I can detect a chronological or procedural contradiction.
I can compare two plausible orders and justify the stronger one.
I can read the final sequence as one coherent paragraph.
I can complete practice items efficiently within the shared reading-section time.
I can classify my errors and select a targeted drill for improvement.
strategy_notes: The opening sentence is usually independent, but independence alone is not enough; it must also introduce the paragraph's central direction.
A proper noun or full technical term often appears before a shorter reference such as the scientist, the theory, or this process.
A pronoun may refer to an entire previous event or claim, not only to the nearest noun.
Definite articles are useful clues, but some nouns are naturally definite because they are unique or contextually obvious.
Demonstratives such as this and these are especially powerful because they usually point to recently presented information.
The phrase 'for example' normally points backward to a generalization, while 'therefore' points backward to evidence or a cause.
Academic writers often introduce a study before its method, present results before interpreting them, and interpret findings before making recommendations.
When one sentence introduces two items, later references such as the former and the latter can create a fixed order.
A strong pair supported by reference plus meaning is safer than a pair supported by topic similarity alone.
The final sentence often gives a consequence, recommendation, evaluation, summary, or completed stage; it should not introduce a major unexplained topic.
Do not translate every sentence word by word. Focus on sentence function, key nouns, references, and logical relationships.
Partial progress matters during practice: track how many adjacent pairs were correct even when the entire order was not perfect.
When uncertain, preserve the highest-confidence links and decide only the boundary between the resulting blocks.
After practice, explain the correct order aloud or in writing; explanation converts passive recognition into a repeatable strategy.
